steps.name: Job
steps.why: On the test it sits beside the passage, above the choices, and its wording is fixed. It tells you which job you are doing and which sentence matters most.

steps.name: Chunk
steps.do: Read one sentence, stop, tag it.
steps.why: Give it one of five tags and say it in plain words. If the sentence is long, find its core first. Mark every turn word.

steps.name: Say
steps.do: Say your own answer before you look at the choices.
steps.why: One line, in the pattern for the job. If you cannot say it, go back to the Point sentence, not to the choices.

steps.name: Check
steps.do: Test each choice against the passage.
steps.why: Split the choice into pieces. Every piece needs a line you can point to, and the whole choice has to do the job. One false piece and it is out.

routineAfter: The five tags. Scene · Old idea · Did · Found · Point. For stories and poems: Scene · Happens · Feeling. For notes, the last line (“The student wants to …”) is the Goal.
The turn words. but · however · although · though · yet · despite · whereas.

Time. The test allows 32 minutes for 27 questions in each module, about 71 seconds a question. The split shown beside the steps is a starting point to adjust as you practice. It is a suggestion, not something measured from the bank.

shape.intro: This is why the plan is built on sentences and not on speed-reading a long text.
bullets: Short passages. The median Information and Ideas passage is 88 words. 90% are 114 words or fewer, only 10 of 555 run past 130, and the longest is 160. 91% have two to five sentences.
Long sentences. Of the 1,937 sentences in those passages, 224 are 40 words or longer. They turn up in 191 passages, 34% of the total.

What difficulty adds. From Easy to Hard the passage grows by a little over a third. The answer choices nearly double in length, and the share of passages holding a 40-word sentence goes from about 1 in 12 to more than half.
Three kinds of passage. 48% report a study (researchers, a team, an experiment). 13% are stories, poems or plays. The remaining 39% explain something in history, the arts or science without a study.

Hard terms are often explained on the spot. 33% of passages define a term inside the passage, in brackets or between dashes. 21% name a research team (“and colleagues,” “et al.”). You do not need to hold on to either: read the names as “the team” and a bracket as “in other words.”
The longest thing you will read is a pair of texts. In Cross-Text Connections the two texts together run 136 words at the median and 170 at most.

jobs.name: Main idea
says: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
jobs.look: Everything. No sentence can be skipped: the answer has to cover the whole passage, not one part of it.

jobs.name: Detail
says: According to the text, why …?
Based on the text, …?
What does the text most strongly suggest about …?
It can most reasonably be inferred from the text that …?
jobs.look: The words the question names. Find them in the passage and read that sentence and its neighbors: the answer restates what is said there. It can be anywhere. In the 32 “According to the text” questions the sentence closest to the answer was first 31% of the time, in the middle 53% and last 16%, about what chance would give. “Inferred” with no blank is still Detail; Inference questions end in a blank (“most logically completes the text”).

jobs.name: Inference
says: Which choice most logically completes the text?
jobs.look: The words just before the blank. The blank ends the last sentence in all 140, and in 138 of them the last sentence carries a logic cue that tells you what kind of statement to supply.

jobs.name: Support
says: Which finding, if true, would most directly support …?
jobs.look: The claim: the sentence with claim, hypothesize, conclude, argue or predict. It is the last sentence in 70 of 83 support and weaken questions. When the passage ends by describing the experiment (11 of 83), the claim comes just before that description.

jobs.name: Weaken
says: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken …?
… undermine …? · … challenge …?
jobs.look: The claim, found the same way as for Support.

jobs.name: Quotation
says: Which quotation from … most effectively illustrates the claim?
Which quotation … would most directly support the student’s claim?
jobs.look: The claim. In all 40 questions about a literary work it is the last sentence, the one that ends in the blank. Count its parts: in 9 of the 40 the claim names a pair that must both show up in the quotation (0 Easy, 6 Medium, 3 Hard).

jobs.name: Table or graph
says: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the researchers’ conclusion?
jobs.look: The sentence with the blank (82 questions, and the blank is always the end of the passage) or, when there is no blank, the claim (46 questions). Decide which rows and columns it needs before you read any numbers. The no-blank kind is harder: 57% of them are Hard, against 29% of the fill-in kind. The other 5 (all Easy) are plain look-ups with no blank and no claim.

jobs.name: Word
says: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
As used in the text, what does the word … most nearly mean?
jobs.look: The sentence that holds the blank or the word, and any turn word in it.

jobs.name: Purpose or structure
says: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

jobs.name: Two texts
says: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to …?
Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
jobs.look: The Point of each text, then how the second stands toward the first.

jobs.name: Notes
says: Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
jobs.look: The goal sentence at the end of the notes: “The student wants to …”

jobIntro: The wording of the question barely changes from test to test. Read it before the passage. It tells you what you will have to produce and where the sentence that matters usually sits.
The first seven jobs are Information and Ideas. The last four are the other reading skills, covered on the page The other reading questions.

leadin.title: Inference: the words before the blank

blocks.p: In 138 of the 140 inference questions the last sentence contains one of these cue words. The cue tells you which way the reasoning runs.

head: The last sentence
Questions
So the blank is
rows: The evidence shows“… suggesting that ___” · “This suggests that ___” · “implies that ___”
What the facts just given point to.
Someone concludes“The researchers concluded that ___” · “hypothesized that ___”
What they would conclude from those facts.
What follows from the sentence before.
A reason“… because ___” · “in that ___” · “the fact that ___”
The cause of what was just said. A reason, not a result.

blocks.p: After each sentence, stop. Give it one tag and say it in about ten words. Only then read the next sentence. This is what keeps you from reaching the end with nothing in your head.

rows.def: Background: who, what, where, when, or what a term means. Usually the opening.is a … · a date · a definition in brackets
What people thought, assumed or claimed before.thought · believed · assumed · argued · typically · traditionally · Some researchers …
What someone did to find out.To test … · To study … · analyzed · compared · examined · collected
What turned out to be true: a result, a fact, an example.found that · showed · numbers · For example,
The claim or conclusion, the author’s or the researchers’.concluded · claims · hypothesize · suggests that · therefore
Who and where. Often the introduction printed before the passage.The following text is from …
What someone feels, wants, thinks or is like. Questions about stories ask about this.

blocks.p: One sentence, two tags. If the two halves of a sentence do different jobs, such as an old idea and then a finding, cut it at the semicolon, at “, and”, at the turn word, or at a comma that adds a comment on the whole clause (“…, a result explicable …”), and tag each half.

Why the tags pay off. 412 of the 555 Information and Ideas questions turn on one claim sentence: the inference, support, weaken and quotation questions, and the 128 table or graph questions that end in a blank or state a claim. Tagging is how you know which sentence that is.
A turn word tells you the passage is about to go somewhere its first part did not. Mark every one.

list: The words. but, however, although, though, yet, despite, whereas, by contrast, nonetheless. “But” alone accounts for 184 of the 323 turn words in these passages; “however” for 58 and “although” for 31.

What comes after the turn carries the weight. Of 23 inference questions read one by one, 14 had a real turn, and in all 14 the answer depended on what came at or after it. In 280 bank passages annotated line by line, the annotators marked a turn in 140, and the answer used a line at or after it in 132, often with a line before it too; turns come early, so chance alone gives about 124. See it by job.
“Although X, Y.” The weight is on Y, the part after the comma. X is true but is not the point.
Old idea, then a turn, then a finding. The finding goes against the old idea. Expect the question to ask about that.
Not every “but” is a turn. In “produced by the eggs of cane toads but not by the eggs of native amphibians,” it only joins two halves of one fact. Ask what is being set against what.

blocks.p: A sentence of 40 words is almost never one long thought. It is a short core with pieces attached. In the 224 sentences of 40 words or more, 97% carry at least one of the attachments below, and the typical one carries two.

head: Attachment, and how to spot it
In sentences of 40+ words
Under 25 words
rows: A second statement joined ona semicolon, a colon, or a comma plus but, and, while, whereas, though
An asidebetween two dashes, or inside brackets
A report framesomeone found, showed, argued or concluded that …
A lead-in before the subjectthe sentence opens with To, Although, By, When, In, Using … and a comma follows
A which or who add-ona comma, then which, who, whose or where
A list of examplessuch as, including, for example

blocks.p: Counted by pattern matching across 224 long and 1,122 short sentences, so read the shares as approximate.
Core first. Use this on any sentence that runs past three lines.

list: If the sentence opens with To, Although, When, By, In or an -ing word, jump to the first comma. The subject is right after it. A typical lead-in is 10 words. (Older texts may leave the comma out: then look for where the subject starts, as in “he would look in”.)
Step over anything between two dashes, between two commas, or in brackets, unless it comes right after a word you do not know: then it is that word’s definition, so read it at once.
Find who did what. If the verb is found, showed, argued, concluded or suggests, the real content is the that part: find who does what inside it.
Say the core in about ten words.

Go back for the pieces you stepped over and ask what each one adds: why, where, when, how, a definition, an example, a limit. Do not drop them for good. The detail a question turns on is often in one of them.

blocks.p: The longest sentence in these 555 questions has 111 words (question 36e2868f, from a novel). Its subject takes 11 words, then 60 words sit between two dashes, and only then does the verb arrive. Lift out what is between the dashes and the sentence is easy.

list: Names of researchers. Read “Yuzo R. Yanagisuru, Otar Akanyeti, and James C. Liao” as “the team.” Questions name them only so you can find the right sentence.
Latin names. Read Astyanax mexicanus as “the fish.” After its first use the passage shortens it anyway (A. mexicanus).
Brackets and dashes after a strange word. They hold its meaning: “vortices (patterns of swirls).” If the word is new to you, the bracket is the first thing to read, not the last.
Old-fashioned wording in stories. Swap in plain words as you go: “want of company” is lack of company; “was desirous to avoid them” is wanted to avoid them.

tagset.title: Five ways a choice is wrong

rows.def: Says something the passage never says. It often sounds reasonable, which is the trap.
Says the reverse of the passage. On support questions: a result that would do the reverse of what is asked.
Uses the passage’s own words but changes what they say, or turns “some” and “may” into “all” and “will.”
True or believable, but it does not answer this question: a finding that does not bear on the claim, a quotation that does not show it, a correct reading of the wrong row.
States something the table or graph does not show.

list: Inference, main idea, detail. The usual wrong choice says something the passage never says. Defense: point to the line. If you cannot, it is out.
Support, weaken, quotation. The usual wrong choice is on the right topic but does not bear on the claim. Defense: your Say line. Hold each choice up to it.
Table or graph. Two checks, in this order. Is the statement true of the data? Then: is it the comparison the claim needs? On Hard questions all four choices can pass the first check.
Down to two choices? Find the one piece where they differ and look for that piece alone in the passage. This is advice, not a measurement.

blocks.p: A wrong choice often has something right in it: a true first half, one part of a two-part claim, or an accurate reading of the data. In the sample that was so for 44% of wrong main-idea choices, table or graph 35%, quotation 31%, detail 21%, inference 7%, support and weaken 7%. College Board’s own explanations grant something true about 18% of the 1,650 wrong choices in the 550 Information and Ideas questions that have a blank or a claim (14% on Easy questions, 19% on Medium, 19% on Hard). So read a choice to its end before you accept it.
Choices grow a second half as questions get harder. Share of answer choices that join two statements, with the median length of a choice:
A choice counts as two-part if it opens with although or while, or joins two statements with but, whereas, and, which or a semicolon. Counted by pattern, so approximate.
Each of these was tested on the Information and Ideas questions. None of them points to the answer.

list: Picking by length. The correct choice is the longest of the four in 19% of questions and the shortest in 17%. Chance is about 25%.

Picking the careful-sounding choice. Cautious words (may, some, often, likely) appear in 29.6% of correct choices and 27.5% of wrong ones. Strong words (all, only, never, most) appear in 15.3% and 15.7%.
Picking the choice that repeats the passage’s words. The correct choice shares the most words with the passage in 18% of questions and the fewest in 21%. Chance is about 25% for each.
Picking by letter. A 27.7%, B 25.2%, C 22.5%, D 24.5%.

Expecting “true but too narrow” on main idea questions. College Board describes only 15 of 186 wrong main-idea choices (8%) as a detail or as not the main focus. Far more often the wrong choice says something the passage does not say.

intro: The choices are written to sound right. Your own line is what you measure them against, so say it before you read them.

head: Job
Say this before the choices
rows: The subject, plus what the passage says about it. If there is a turn, give both sides: “X, but Y.”
The answer to the question, taken from the sentence that holds its key words.
Finish the last sentence yourself. After “suggesting that” or “therefore”: what follows. After “because”: the reason.
“I need a result that shows …” Restate the claim as A leads to B or A more than B, then say what result would show it.
“I need the cause without the effect, or the effect without the cause.” For a comparison: the two groups coming out equal, or the other way round.
“The quotation must show (1) … and (2) …” Number the parts of the claim.
“I need this row compared across these columns.” Name the comparison before you look at the numbers.
Your own plain word for the blank.
Your tags in order: “an old idea, then a finding against it.”
One line per text, then: agrees, disagrees, or “yes, but.”
The goal in your own words, and which notes it calls for.

examples.title: Main idea
examples.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
examples.jobans: There is no shortcut for this job: every sentence counts, so tag each one.

chunks.html: The painter María Izquierdo played an important role in the development of twentieth-century Mexican art, <mark class="turn">but</mark> her work has never been well-known in the United States except among art historians.
chunks.text: The painter María Izquierdo played an important role in the development of twentieth-century Mexican art, but her work has never been well-known in the United States except among art historians.
chunks.plain: She mattered in Mexican art, but few people in the US know her work.

chunks.html: One reason for Izquierdo’s relative obscurity is the enormous popularity of some of her peers.
chunks.text: One reason for Izquierdo’s relative obscurity is the enormous popularity of some of her peers.
chunks.plain: Why: other painters of her time are hugely popular.

chunks.html: In particular, the painters Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera have so captivated the interest of US audiences that Izquierdo and other Mexican artists from the period often get overlooked, <mark class="turn">despite</mark> the high quality of their work.
chunks.text: In particular, the painters Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera have so captivated the interest of US audiences that Izquierdo and other Mexican artists from the period often get overlooked, despite the high quality of their work.
chunks.plain: Kahlo and Rivera hold the attention, so good artists like her get overlooked.

examples.say: Izquierdo deserves to be known in the US but is not, because Kahlo and Rivera take the attention.

choices.t: Izquierdo’s work is not as well-known in the United States as it should be because Kahlo and Rivera draw so much of the public’s attention.
choices.why: Both halves have a line to point to: “never been well-known in the United States” (sentence 1) with “overlooked, despite the high quality of their work” (sentence 3), and “Kahlo and Rivera have so captivated the interest of US audiences” (sentence 3).

choices.t: During Izquierdo’s lifetime, her paintings were displayed in galleries in the United States much more frequently than paintings by Kahlo and Rivera were.
choices.why: Nothing is said about galleries during her lifetime.

choices.t: Izquierdo painted some of the same subjects that Kahlo and Rivera painted but used different techniques than they used.
choices.why: Her subjects and techniques never come up.

choices.t: Few of Izquierdo’s works are in galleries today because she produced only a small number of paintings.
choices.why: How many paintings she made never comes up.

examples.lesson: Take away. All three wrong choices are about things the passage never mentions. None of them is a true detail that is merely too small. That is the usual pattern for main idea questions.

examples.title: Main idea
examples.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
examples.jobans: Two sentences, both long, so take each one core first.

chunks.html: Several scholars have argued that conditions in England in the late ninth through early eleventh centuries—namely, burgeoning literacy amid running conflicts between England’s Anglo-Saxon kingdoms and Danish invaders—were especially conducive to the production of the Old English epic poem Beowulf, and they have dated the poem’s composition accordingly.
chunks.text: Several scholars have argued that conditions in England in the late ninth through early eleventh centuries —namely, burgeoning literacy amid running conflicts between England’s Anglo-Saxon kingdoms and Danish invaders— were especially conducive to the production of the Old English epic poem Beowulf, and they have dated the poem’s composition accordingly.
chunks.plain: Some scholars: England in the 800s to 1000s suited Beowulf, so they date the poem to then.

chunks.html: It is not inconceivable that Beowulf emerged from such a context, <mark class="turn">but</mark> privileging contextual fit over the linguistic evidence of an eighth- or even seventh-century composition requires a level of justification that thus far has not been presented.
chunks.text: It is not inconceivable that Beowulf emerged from such a context, but privileging contextual fit over the linguistic evidence of an eighth- or even seventh-century composition requires a level of justification that thus far has not been presented.
chunks.plain: That is possible. But the language points to an earlier date, and nobody has justified setting that aside.

examples.say: The late date is possible, but its supporters have not dealt with the language evidence for an earlier date.

choices.t: Although there are some grounds for believing that Beowulf was composed between the late ninth and early eleventh centuries, advocates for that view tend to rely on evidence that has been called into question by advocates for an earlier date.
choices.why: The passage says these scholars skip over other evidence. It does not say their own evidence has been called into question.

choices.t: Although several scholars have dated Beowulf to the late ninth through early eleventh centuries, others have argued that doing so privileges a controversial interpretation of the social conditions of the period.
choices.why: No controversy about how to read the period is mentioned.

choices.t: Although Beowulf fits well with the historical context of England in the late ninth through early eleventh centuries, it fits equally well with the historical context of England in the seventh and eighth centuries.
choices.why: The earlier date rests on the language of the poem. Nothing is said about how well the earlier period fits.

choices.t: Although the claim of a late ninth- through early eleventh-century composition date for Beowulf has some plausibility, advocates for the claim have not compellingly addressed evidence suggesting an earlier date.
choices.why: “Some plausibility” matches “not inconceivable.” “Have not compellingly addressed evidence suggesting an earlier date” matches “a level of justification that thus far has not been presented.”

examples.lesson: Take away. All four choices open with the same true “Although” half. On Hard questions the second half decides, so test it word by word. Note the double negative: “not inconceivable” means possible.

examples.title: Detail
examples.question: According to the text, why does Bill regularly ask about “seafaring men”?
examples.jobans: The question names its subject: why Bill asks about “seafaring men.” Find that phrase, then read on for the reason.

chunks.html: The following text is adapted from Robert Louis Stevenson’s 1883 novel Treasure Island.
chunks.text: The following text is adapted from Robert Louis Stevenson’s 1883 novel Treasure Island.
chunks.plain: A passage from a novel.

chunks.html: Bill is a sailor staying at the Admiral Benbow, an inn run by the narrator’s parents.
chunks.text: Bill is a sailor staying at the Admiral Benbow, an inn run by the narrator’s parents.
chunks.plain: Bill, a sailor, is staying at the inn run by the narrator’s family.

chunks.html: Every day when [Bill] came back from his stroll he would ask if any seafaring men had gone by along the road.
chunks.text: Every day when [Bill] came back from his stroll he would ask if any seafaring men had gone by along the road.
chunks.plain: Every day Bill asks whether any sailors have passed by.

chunks.html: At first we thought it was the want of company of his own kind that made him ask this question, <mark class="turn">but</mark> at last we began to see he was desirous to avoid them.
chunks.text: At first we thought it was the want of company of his own kind that made him ask this question, but at last we began to see he was desirous to avoid them.
chunks.plain: We first thought he missed other sailors. In fact he wanted to avoid them.

chunks.html: When a seaman did [stay] at the Admiral Benbow (as now and then some did) he would look in at him through the curtained door before he entered the parlour; and he was always sure to be as silent as a mouse when any such was present.
chunks.text: When a seaman did [stay] at the Admiral Benbow (as now and then some did) he would look in at him through the curtained door before he entered the parlour; and he was always sure to be as silent as a mouse when any such was present.
chunks.plain: When a sailor does come in, Bill peeks at him first and keeps silent.

examples.say: He wants to keep away from other sailors.

choices.t: He’s hoping to find an old friend and fellow sailor.
choices.why: This is the narrator’s first guess, the part before “but.” The passage then corrects it, which is why it tempts.

choices.t: He’s trying to secure a job as part of the crew on a new ship.
choices.why: Nothing about looking for work on a ship.

choices.t: He isn’t sure that other guests at the inn will be welcoming of sailors.
choices.why: Nothing about how other guests treat sailors.

choices.t: He doesn’t want to encounter any other sailor unexpectedly.
choices.why: “Desirous to avoid them,” and he checks through the door before going in.

examples.lesson: Take away. The trap is the idea that comes before the turn. “At first we thought … but at last we began to see”: the answer is after “but.” Older wording to put in plain words: “want of company” is lack of company.

examples.title: Detail
examples.question: It can most reasonably be inferred from the text that the finding about the microorganism community composition was important for which reason?
examples.jobans: The question names its subject: the finding about “microorganism community composition.” Find it and read what the passage says it allowed.

chunks.html: To understand how temperature change affects microorganism-mediated cycling of soil nutrients in alpine ecosystems, Eva Kaštovská et al. collected plant-soil cores in the Tatra Mountains at elevations around 2,100 meters and transplanted them to elevations of 1,700–1,800 meters, where the mean air temperature was warmer by 2°C.
chunks.text: To understand how temperature change affects microorganism-mediated cycling of soil nutrients in alpine ecosystems, Eva Kaštovská et al. collected plant-soil cores in the Tatra Mountains at elevations around 2,100 meters and transplanted them to elevations of 1,700–1,800 meters, where the mean air temperature was warmer by 2°C.
chunks.plain: They moved soil cores downhill, to where the air is 2°C warmer.

chunks.html: Microorganism-mediated nutrient cycling was accelerated in the transplanted cores;
chunks.text: Microorganism-mediated nutrient cycling was accelerated in the transplanted cores;
chunks.plain: Nutrient cycling sped up in the moved cores.

chunks.html: crucially, microorganism community composition was unchanged, allowing Kaštovská et al. to attribute the acceleration to temperature-induced increases in microorganism activity.
chunks.text: crucially, microorganism community composition was unchanged, allowing Kaštovská et al. to attribute the acceleration to temperature-induced increases in microorganism activity.
chunks.plain: The mix of microbes did not change, so the speed-up must come from the same microbes working harder in the warmth.

examples.say: Because the microbes were the same ones, a change in which microbes were present cannot be the cause. Only the warmth is left.

choices.t: It provided preliminary evidence that microorganism-mediated nutrient cycling was accelerated in the transplanted cores.
choices.why: The speed-up is in the passage, but this finding is not the evidence for it. It explains the cause.

choices.t: It suggested that temperature-induced changes in microorganism activity may be occurring at increasingly high elevations.
choices.why: Nothing about changes reaching higher and higher elevations.

choices.t: It ruled out a potential alternative explanation for the acceleration in microorganism-mediated nutrient cycling.
choices.why: “Unchanged, allowing [them] to attribute the acceleration to temperature”: the finding removes the other possible cause.

choices.t: It clarified that microorganism activity levels in the plant-soil cores varied depending on which microorganisms comprised the community.
choices.why: Nothing about activity differing by which microbes are present. The mix stayed the same.

examples.lesson: Take away. “Crucially … allowing them to attribute” is a signal. When a passage calls a fact important, ask what the researchers could not have concluded without it.

examples.title: Inference
examples.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
examples.jobans: Look at the words just before the blank: “suggesting that.” The blank is what the evidence shows.

chunks.html: Herbivorous sauropod dinosaurs could grow more than 100 feet long and weigh up to 80 tons,
chunks.text: Herbivorous sauropod dinosaurs could grow more than 100 feet long and weigh up to 80 tons,
chunks.plain: Sauropods were enormous.

chunks.html: and some researchers have attributed the evolution of sauropods to such massive sizes to increased plant production resulting from high levels of atmospheric carbon dioxide during the Mesozoic era.
chunks.text: and some researchers have attributed the evolution of sauropods to such massive sizes to increased plant production resulting from high levels of atmospheric carbon dioxide during the Mesozoic era.
chunks.plain: Some researchers say: high carbon dioxide meant more plants, and that made sauropods giant.

chunks.html: However, there is no evidence of significant spikes in carbon dioxide levels coinciding with relevant periods in sauropod evolution, such as when the first large sauropods appeared, when several sauropod lineages underwent further evolution toward gigantism, or when sauropods reached their maximum known sizes, suggesting that ______
chunks.text: However , there is no evidence of significant spikes in carbon dioxide levels coinciding with relevant periods in sauropod evolution, such as when the first large sauropods appeared, when several sauropod lineages underwent further evolution toward gigantism, or when sauropods reached their maximum known sizes, suggesting that ______
chunks.plain: But carbon dioxide did not spike at any of the key moments. So …

examples.say: … growing huge did not depend on high carbon dioxide.

choices.t: fluctuations in atmospheric carbon dioxide affected different sauropod lineages differently.
choices.why: No fluctuations are described, and nothing about different lineages reacting differently.

choices.t: the evolution of larger body sizes in sauropods did not depend on increased atmospheric carbon dioxide.
choices.why: No spike at the first large sauropods, at the further growth, or at the maximum size: the growth happened without the supposed cause.

choices.t: atmospheric carbon dioxide was higher when the largest known sauropods lived than it was when the first sauropods appeared.
choices.why: The passage says there were no significant spikes at those moments.

choices.t: sauropods probably would not have evolved to such immense sizes if atmospheric carbon dioxide had been even slightly higher.
choices.why: Nothing about what even higher levels would have done.

examples.lesson: Take away. Old idea, then “However,” then evidence: the evidence goes against the old idea, and the blank says so. The three-part “such as when …” list can be skipped on the first read.

examples.title: Inference
examples.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
examples.jobans: The words before the blank are “suggesting that,” so the blank is what the last finding points to.

chunks.html: Some Astyanax mexicanus, a river-dwelling fish found in northeast Mexico, have colonized caves in the region.
chunks.text: Some Astyanax mexicanus, a river-dwelling fish found in northeast Mexico, have colonized caves in the region.
chunks.plain: Some of these river fish now live in caves.

chunks.html: Although there is little genetic difference between river and cave A. mexicanus and all members of the species can emit the same sounds, biologist Carole Hyacinthe and colleagues found that the context and significance of those sounds vary by location—e.g., the click that river-dwelling A. mexicanus use to signal aggression is used by cave dwellers when foraging—and the acoustic properties of cave fish sounds show some cave-specific variations as well.
chunks.text: Although there is little genetic difference between river and cave A. mexicanus and all members of the species can emit the same sounds, biologist Carole Hyacinthe and colleagues found that the context and significance of those sounds vary by location —e.g., the click that river-dwelling A. mexicanus use to signal aggression is used by cave dwellers when foraging— and the acoustic properties of cave fish sounds show some cave-specific variations as well.
chunks.plain: Same genes and same sounds. But river fish and cave fish use the sounds for different things.

chunks.html: Hyacinthe and colleagues note that differences in sonic communication could accumulate to the point of inhibiting interbreeding among fish from different locations, suggesting that ______
chunks.text: Hyacinthe and colleagues note that differences in sonic communication could accumulate to the point of inhibiting interbreeding among fish from different locations, suggesting that ______
chunks.plain: These differences could grow until the groups stop interbreeding. So …

examples.say: … one species now may be on its way to becoming separate groups.

choices.t: although A. mexicanus living in rivers are genetically similar to those living in caves, river fish rely on sonic communication less than cave fish do.
choices.why: First half true. Nothing says river fish rely on sound less.

choices.t: although A. mexicanus is a single species at present, it could be in the process of splitting into distinct populations with different characteristics.
choices.why: “Little genetic difference” gives the first half (one species now). “Could accumulate to the point of inhibiting interbreeding” gives the second (may be splitting).

choices.t: although all A. mexicanus emit sounds, the fish living in rivers produce some sounds that the fish living in caves do not, and vice versa.
choices.why: First half true. But all members “can emit the same sounds”; only the use differs.

choices.t: although A. mexicanus from different locations can interbreed currently, river fish and cave fish are sufficiently genetically distinct that they can be considered separate species.
choices.why: First half fits. But the passage says there is “little genetic difference.”

examples.lesson: Take away. Every choice opens with a true “although” half. Go straight to the second half and test that.

examples.title: Support
examples.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the second research team’s hypothesis?
examples.jobans: Find the claim: “has therefore hypothesized that …” in the last sentence. It contains “less likely than,” so two groups are being compared.

chunks.html: Water flowing around an obstruction creates vortices (patterns of swirls) of varying size; by detecting the vortices, fish can determine the size and position of the obstruction.
chunks.text: Water flowing around an obstruction creates vortices (patterns of swirls) of varying size; by detecting the vortices, fish can determine the size and position of the obstruction.
chunks.plain: Obstacles make swirls in water. Fish sense the swirls to locate the obstacle.

chunks.html: Testing by Yuzo R. Yanagisuru, Otar Akanyeti, and James C. Liao using models of three head shapes—narrow (low ratio of width to length), intermediate, and wide (high ratio of width to length)—showed that for medium-sized vortices, fish with wide heads would be least able to distinguish between vortices and general turbulence in the water.
chunks.text: Testing by Yuzo R. Yanagisuru, Otar Akanyeti, and James C. Liao using models of three head shapes —narrow (low ratio of width to length), intermediate, and wide (high ratio of width to length)— showed that for medium-sized vortices, fish with wide heads would be least able to distinguish between vortices and general turbulence in the water.
chunks.plain: Model tests: wide-headed fish are the worst at telling swirls from ordinary turbulence.

chunks.html: A second research team has therefore hypothesized that in low-visibility conditions, wider-headed fish will be less likely than narrower-headed fish to detect obstructions.
chunks.text: A second research team has therefore hypothesized that in low-visibility conditions, wider-headed fish will be less likely than narrower-headed fish to detect obstructions.
chunks.plain: Hypothesis: when they cannot see well, wide-headed fish detect obstacles less often than narrow-headed fish.

examples.say: I need a result where wide-headed fish hit obstacles more often than narrow-headed fish, in the same conditions.

choices.t: A study using obstructions that created medium-sized vortices in low-visibility conditions found that the bristlemouth (Chaetostoma yurubiense), which has a relatively wide head, bumped into more than half of the obstructions.
choices.why: Only wide-headed fish. With no narrow-headed fish there is nothing to compare.

choices.t: A study using obstructions that created medium-sized vortices in low-visibility conditions found that some specimens of dusky smooth-hound (Mustelus canis), which has a relatively narrow head, bumped into the obstructions more often than other specimens of the same fish did.
choices.why: Compares fish inside one narrow-headed species. Head width does not vary.

choices.t: A study using obstructions that created medium-sized vortices in low-visibility conditions found that the wider-headed bristlemouth (Chaetostoma yurubiense) bumped into obstructions more often than the narrower-headed dusky smooth-hound (Mustelus canis) did.
choices.why: Wide-headed against narrow-headed, same conditions, and the wide-headed fish do worse.

choices.t: A study using obstructions that created medium-sized vortices in low-visibility conditions found that the narrower-headed dusky smooth-hound (Mustelus canis) bumped into the obstructions just as often as the wider-headed bristlemouth (Chaetostoma yurubiense) did.
choices.why: Equal rates would count against the hypothesis.

examples.lesson: Take away. A claim with “than” needs both sides in the answer. A result about one group alone cannot support it.

examples.title: Support
examples.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ conclusion?
examples.jobans: The claim is the last sentence: “The researchers concluded that …” Underline what it measures: total pollen.

chunks.html: In subtropical Asia, Apis dorsata (giant honeybee) plays an essential role in pollinating a wide variety of crops and wild plants.
chunks.text: In subtropical Asia, Apis dorsata (giant honeybee) plays an essential role in pollinating a wide variety of crops and wild plants.
chunks.plain: Giant honeybees pollinate many crops and wild plants.

chunks.html: To study how different agricultural land covers affect the species, Rika Raffiudin and colleagues monitored the foraging activity of the bees as well as the pollen content of the honey from A. dorsata colonies at two sites in Indonesia: Kampar, characterized by its surrounding monoculture farms (growing a single crop), and Kerinci, a forest-agriculture site where multiple crops, including hot peppers and coffee, are grown nearby.
chunks.text: To study how different agricultural land covers affect the species, Rika Raffiudin and colleagues monitored the foraging activity of the bees as well as the pollen content of the honey from A. dorsata colonies at two sites in Indonesia: Kampar, characterized by its surrounding monoculture farms (growing a single crop), and Kerinci, a forest-agriculture site where multiple crops, including hot peppers and coffee, are grown nearby.
chunks.plain: They watched bees and tested honey at two sites: Kampar (one crop) and Kerinci (many crops).

chunks.html: The researchers concluded that a lack of crop variety may reduce total pollen collection by A. dorsata.
chunks.text: The researchers concluded that a lack of crop variety may reduce total pollen collection by A. dorsata.
chunks.plain: Conclusion: fewer kinds of crop may mean less pollen collected in total.

examples.say: I need Kampar (one crop) to show less pollen in total than Kerinci (many crops).

choices.t: Pollen in honey samples from Kampar bee colonies was predominantly sourced from a single plant species, whereas pollen in honey samples from Kerinci bee colonies was sourced from multiple different plant species.
choices.why: About how many kinds of pollen, not how much. This is the tempting one.

choices.t: In one Kerinci bee colony, a greater proportion of bees returned to their nests with pollen than returned without pollen, whereas the inverse was observed in a second Kerinci bee colony.
choices.why: Two colonies at the same site. Crop variety does not differ between them.

choices.t: Significantly fewer bees were observed engaging in foraging activities with the crops surrounding Kerinci than with the crops surrounding Kampar.
choices.why: Counts bees, not pollen: it says nothing about how much pollen was collected.

choices.t: Honey samples from Kerinci bee colonies contained significantly higher concentrations of pollen than honey samples from Kampar bee colonies did.
choices.why: More pollen in the honey at the many-crop site than at the one-crop site.

examples.lesson: Take away. Underline the thing the claim measures. Choice A matches the topic (variety of crops) but measures the wrong thing (variety of pollen).

examples.title: Weaken
examples.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the team’s hypothesis?
examples.jobans: The claim is the last sentence: “hypothesized that …” It is a cause-and-effect claim: yellow carbon plus blue ice makes green.

chunks.html: Icebergs generally appear to be mostly white or blue, depending on how the ice reflects sunlight.
chunks.text: Icebergs generally appear to be mostly white or blue, depending on how the ice reflects sunlight.
chunks.plain: Icebergs usually look white or blue.

chunks.html: Ice with air bubbles trapped in it looks white because much of the light reflects off the bubbles.
chunks.text: Ice with air bubbles trapped in it looks white because much of the light reflects off the bubbles.
chunks.plain: Bubbles in the ice: white.

chunks.html: Ice without air bubbles usually looks blue because the light travels deep into the ice and only a little of it is reflected.
chunks.text: Ice without air bubbles usually looks blue because the light travels deep into the ice and only a little of it is reflected.
chunks.plain: No bubbles: blue.

chunks.html: <mark class="turn">However</mark>, some icebergs in the sea around Antarctica appear to be green.
chunks.text: However , some icebergs in the sea around Antarctica appear to be green.
chunks.plain: But some Antarctic icebergs are green.

chunks.html: One team of scientists hypothesized that this phenomenon is the result of yellow-tinted dissolved organic carbon in Antarctic waters mixing with blue ice to produce the color green.
chunks.text: One team of scientists hypothesized that this phenomenon is the result of yellow-tinted dissolved organic carbon in Antarctic waters mixing with blue ice to produce the color green.
chunks.plain: Hypothesis: yellow carbon in the water mixes with blue ice and makes green.

examples.say: To weaken it I need the cause without the effect: blue icebergs with just as much carbon. Or green icebergs without the carbon.

choices.t: White ice doesn’t change color when mixed with dissolved organic carbon due to the air bubbles in the ice.
choices.why: About white ice. The hypothesis is about blue ice.

choices.t: Dissolved organic carbon has a stronger yellow color in Antarctic waters than it does in other places.
choices.why: Compares Antarctica with other places. It says nothing about whether carbon turns ice green.

choices.t: Blue icebergs and green icebergs are rarely found near each other.
choices.why: This fits the hypothesis: where the carbon is, blue ice would turn green.

choices.t: Blue icebergs and green icebergs contain similarly small traces of dissolved organic carbon.
choices.why: The same carbon in blue and in green icebergs: the cause is present in both, the effect in only one.

examples.lesson: Take away. To weaken a cause-and-effect claim, look for the cause without the effect, or the effect without the cause.

examples.title: Quotation
examples.question: Which quotation from “The Young Girl” most effectively illustrates the claim?
examples.jobans: The claim is the sentence that ends in the blank. Count its parts: pleasant appearance, and unpleasant attitude. Two.

chunks.html: “The Young Girl” is a 1920 short story by Katherine Mansfield.
chunks.text: “The Young Girl” is a 1920 short story by Katherine Mansfield.
chunks.plain: A 1920 short story.

chunks.html: In the story, the narrator takes an unnamed seventeen-year-old girl and her younger brother out for a meal.
chunks.text: In the story, the narrator takes an unnamed seventeen-year-old girl and her younger brother out for a meal.
chunks.plain: The narrator takes a seventeen-year-old girl and her brother out to eat.

chunks.html: In describing the teenager, Mansfield frequently contrasts the character’s pleasant appearance with her unpleasant attitude, as when Mansfield writes of the teenager, ______
chunks.text: In describing the teenager, Mansfield frequently contrasts the character’s pleasant appearance with her unpleasant attitude, as when Mansfield writes of the teenager, ______
chunks.plain: Claim: the writer sets (1) how nice she looks against (2) how sour she acts.

examples.say: The quotation must show both: something pleasant about her looks and something unpleasant about her attitude.

choices.t: “I heard her murmur, ‘I can’t bear flowers on a table.’ They had evidently been giving her intense pain, for she positively closed her eyes as I moved them away.”
choices.why: Part 2 only: she cannot bear the flowers and acts as if they pain her. Nothing about how she looks.

choices.t: “While we waited she took out a little, gold powder-box with a mirror in the lid, shook the poor little puff as though she loathed it, and dabbed her lovely nose.”
choices.why: “Lovely nose” is part 1. “As though she loathed it” is part 2.

choices.t: “I saw, after that, she couldn’t stand this place a moment longer, and, indeed, she jumped up and turned away while I went through the vulgar act of paying for the tea.”
choices.why: Part 2 only: she cannot stand the place. Nothing about her looks.

choices.t: “She didn’t even take her gloves off. She lowered her eyes and drummed on the table. When a faint violin sounded she winced and bit her lip again. Silence.”
choices.why: Part 2 only: she winces and bites her lip. Nothing about her looks.

examples.lesson: Take away. When the claim has two parts, number them and tick each one off inside the quotation. All three wrong choices show only her attitude; none says how she looks.

examples.title: Table or graph
examples.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
examples.jobans: The blank comes after “given that,” so it must be the evidence for the claim, not a conclusion. Decide the comparison before reading the numbers.

chunks.html: After a volcanic eruption spilled lava into North Pacific Ocean waters, a dramatic increase of diatoms (a kind of phytoplankton) near the surface occurred.
chunks.text: After a volcanic eruption spilled lava into North Pacific Ocean waters, a dramatic increase of diatoms (a kind of phytoplankton) near the surface occurred.
chunks.plain: After lava entered the ocean, diatoms boomed near the surface.

chunks.html: Scientists assumed the diatoms were thriving on nutrients such as phosphate from the lava,
chunks.text: Scientists assumed the diatoms were thriving on nutrients such as phosphate from the lava,
chunks.plain: Old idea: the diatoms fed on phosphate from the lava.

chunks.html: <mark class="turn">but</mark> analysis showed these nutrients weren’t present near the surface in forms diatoms can consume.
chunks.text: but analysis showed these nutrients weren’t present near the surface in forms diatoms can consume.
chunks.plain: But that phosphate was not in a form they could use.

chunks.html: <mark class="turn">However</mark>, there was an abundance of usable nitrate, a nutrient usually found in much deeper water and almost never found in lava.
chunks.text: However , there was an abundance of usable nitrate, a nutrient usually found in much deeper water and almost never found in lava.
chunks.plain: There was plenty of usable nitrate, which normally sits deep down and is not in lava.

chunks.html: Microbial oceanographer Sonya Dyhrman and colleagues believe that as the lava plunged nearly 300 meters below the surface it dislodged pockets of this nutrient, releasing it to float upward, given that ______
chunks.text: Microbial oceanographer Sonya Dyhrman and colleagues believe that as the lava plunged nearly 300 meters below the surface it dislodged pockets of this nutrient, releasing it to float upward, given that ______
chunks.plain: Claim: the sinking lava knocked deep nitrate loose and it floated up. Given that …

examples.say: I need nitrate to be higher where the lava was than where it was not.

choices.t: at 5–45 meters below the surface, the average concentration of phosphate was about the same in the seawater in the lava-affected area as in the seawater outside of the lava-affected area.
choices.why: Reads the table correctly (0.17 against 0.14), but it is about phosphate. The claim is about nitrate.

choices.t: for both depth ranges measured, the average concentrations of nitrate were substantially higher in the seawater in the lava-affected area than in the seawater outside of the lava-affected area.
choices.why: Nitrate row: 3.1 and 0.4 in the lava area against ≤0.03 and ≤0.01 outside it.

choices.t: for both depth ranges measured in the seawater in the lava-affected area, the average concentrations of nitrate were substantially higher than the average concentrations of phosphate.
choices.why: Reads the table correctly, but compares nitrate with phosphate, not lava with no lava.

choices.t: in the seawater outside of the lava-affected area, there was little change in the average concentration of nitrate from 75–125 meters below the surface to 5–45 meters below the surface.
choices.why: Reads the table correctly, but looks only at water outside the lava area.

examples.lesson: Take away. All four choices read the table correctly. Only one is the comparison the claim needs. Name the comparison first: which row, which columns.

examples.title: Table or graph
examples.question: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the student’s argument?
examples.jobans: No blank here: the claim is the student’s argument in the last sentence. “Doesn’t entirely explain” means you need a case the explanation cannot reach.

head: Amphibian species (common name)
Percentage of eggs eaten
Native to Australia
Produces bufadienolide

chunks.html: Native to Latin America, the cane toad was introduced to Australia in the 1930s.
chunks.text: Native to Latin America, the cane toad was introduced to Australia in the 1930s.
chunks.plain: Cane toads were brought to Australia in the 1930s.

chunks.html: In recent decades, tadpoles in the Australian population have been shown to consume eggs of their own species.
chunks.text: In recent decades, tadpoles in the Australian population have been shown to consume eggs of their own species.
chunks.plain: Their tadpoles eat cane toad eggs.

chunks.html: A 2022 study showed that when presented with cane toad eggs as well as eggs of native Australian amphibians, cane toad tadpoles disproportionately consumed eggs of their own species.
chunks.text: A 2022 study showed that when presented with cane toad eggs as well as eggs of native Australian amphibians, cane toad tadpoles disproportionately consumed eggs of their own species.
chunks.plain: Given a choice, the tadpoles mostly eat eggs of their own species.

chunks.html: This behavior results from their attraction to bufadienolide, a chemical produced by the eggs of cane toads but not by the eggs of native amphibians.
chunks.text: This behavior results from their attraction to bufadienolide, a chemical produced by the eggs of cane toads but not by the eggs of native amphibians.
chunks.plain: Explanation: they are drawn to a chemical that only cane toad eggs make.

chunks.html: <mark class="turn">However</mark>, using data from this study, a student wishes to argue that the presence of bufadienolide doesn’t entirely explain the cane toad tadpoles’ preference for certain eggs over others.
chunks.text: However , using data from this study, a student wishes to argue that the presence of bufadienolide doesn’t entirely explain the cane toad tadpoles’ preference for certain eggs over others.
chunks.plain: A student argues the chemical is not the whole story.

examples.say: I need a difference the chemical cannot explain: two kinds of eggs that both lack it but were eaten at different rates.

choices.t: The tadpoles consumed a higher percentage of the striped burrowing frog eggs than they did of the eggs of the dainty green tree frog.
choices.why: Striped burrowing frog 10%, dainty green tree frog 1%. Neither produces the chemical, yet one was eaten ten times as often.

choices.t: The tadpoles left a certain percentage of the eggs of each of the five species unharmed, thus ultimately allowing them to hatch.
choices.why: The first half fits the table (no species is at 100%), but nothing in the data says the eggs hatched, and the choice is about eggs left alone, not about preferring some eggs to others.

choices.t: The tadpoles consumed a lower percentage of the short-footed frog eggs than they did of the eggs of their own species.
choices.why: True of the table (7% against 90%), but this is exactly the difference the chemical does explain.

choices.t: The tadpoles consumed the same percentage of the dainty green tree frog eggs as they did of the little red tree frog eggs.
choices.why: True of the table (1% and 1%), but equal rates show no preference at all.

examples.lesson: Take away. When the task is to show that an explanation is incomplete, find a difference among cases where the explanation’s cause is absent.

examples.title: Main idea
examples.question: What is the main idea of the text?
examples.jobans: This one is a poem. Use the literature tags, and put each clause into plain modern words.

chunks.html: The following text is adapted from William Shakespeare’s 1609 poem “Sonnet 27.”
chunks.text: The following text is adapted from William Shakespeare’s 1609 poem “Sonnet 27.”
chunks.plain: A sonnet by Shakespeare.

chunks.html: The poem is addressed to a close friend as if he were physically present.
chunks.text: The poem is addressed to a close friend as if he were physically present.
chunks.plain: The speaker talks to a friend who is not actually there.

chunks.html:
Weary with toil, I [hurry] to my bed,
The dear repose for limbs with travel tired;
chunks.text: Weary with toil, I [hurry] to my bed, The dear repose for limbs with travel tired;
chunks.plain: I am worn out, so I hurry to bed.

chunks.html:
But then begins a journey in my head
To work my mind, when body’s work’s expired:
chunks.text: But then begins a journey in my head To work my mind, when body’s work’s expired:
chunks.plain: But then my mind starts working.

chunks.html:
For then my thoughts—from far where I abide—
[Begin] a zealous pilgrimage to thee,
And keep my drooping eyelids open wide,
chunks.text: For then my thoughts—from far where I abide— [Begin] a zealous pilgrimage to thee, And keep my drooping eyelids open wide,
chunks.plain: My thoughts travel to you and keep my eyes open.

examples.say: He is exhausted, but thinking about his friend keeps him awake.

choices.t: The speaker is asleep and dreaming about traveling to see the friend.
choices.why: He is not asleep. His eyes are kept “open wide.”

choices.t: The speaker is planning an upcoming trip to the friend’s house.
choices.why: The “journey” and “pilgrimage” happen “in my head.” They are a figure of speech for thinking.

choices.t: The speaker is too fatigued to continue a discussion with the friend.
choices.why: No discussion with the friend takes place.

choices.t: The speaker is thinking about the friend instead of immediately falling asleep.
choices.why: “A journey in my head,” thoughts that go “to thee,” and eyelids kept “open wide.”

examples.lesson: Take away. The same routine works on verse. “But then” is the turn: the body rests, the mind does not. Read a figure of speech for what it stands for.

examples.title: Word
examples.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
examples.jobans: The sentence with the blank has a turn word. The blank sits on one side of “but”; the clue is on the other side.

chunks.html: Some scientists have suggested that mammals in the Mesozoic era were not a very ______ group,
chunks.text: Some scientists have suggested that mammals in the Mesozoic era were not a very ______ group,
chunks.plain: Some scientists: Mesozoic mammals were not a very ___ group.

chunks.html: <mark class="turn">but</mark> paleontologist Zhe-Xi Luo’s research suggests that early mammals living in the shadow of dinosaurs weren’t all ground-dwelling insectivores.
chunks.text: but paleontologist Zhe-Xi Luo’s research suggests that early mammals living in the shadow of dinosaurs weren’t all ground-dwelling insectivores.
chunks.plain: But Luo’s research: they were not all one kind of animal.

chunks.html: Fossils of various plant-eating mammals have been found in China, including species like Vilevolodon diplomylos, which Luo says could glide like a flying squirrel.
chunks.text: Fossils of various plant-eating mammals have been found in China, including species like Vilevolodon diplomylos, which Luo says could glide like a flying squirrel.
chunks.plain: Fossils show plant-eaters, and even a glider.

examples.say: My own word for the blank: “varied.”

choices.t: predatory
choices.why: Means hunting other animals. The contrast is about variety, not hunting.

choices.t: obscure
choices.why: Means little known. Nothing in the passage is about how well known they were.

choices.t: diverse
choices.why: “Weren’t all ground-dwelling insectivores” and “various” point to variety.

choices.t: localized
choices.why: Means limited to one area. The clue is about kinds of animal, not places.

examples.lesson: Take away. Put your own plain word in the blank first, then match it. Watch the two negatives: “not very ___” is set against “weren’t all” one kind.

examples.title: Purpose or structure
examples.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
examples.jobans: The answer is the order of your tags, so tag carefully. Both sentences are long: cut each at its joint.

chunks.html: Vadamalai Elangovan and Ganapathi Marimuthu showed that high moonlight intensity inhibits the activity of the greater short-nosed fruit bat (Cynopterus sphinx),
chunks.text: Vadamalai Elangovan and Ganapathi Marimuthu showed that high moonlight intensity inhibits the activity of the greater short-nosed fruit bat (Cynopterus sphinx),
chunks.plain: Bright moonlight makes these fruit bats less active.

chunks.html: a result explicable in terms of benefits and costs: greater lunar intensity may not enable the bats to increase foraging success enough to offset the higher chance of detection by predatory owls or hawks.
chunks.text: a result explicable in terms of benefits and costs: greater lunar intensity may not enable the bats to increase foraging success enough to offset the higher chance of detection by predatory owls or hawks.
chunks.plain: Why: a little more food is not worth being seen by owls and hawks.

chunks.html: Most other nocturnal mammals respond to lunar intensity variations similarly to greater short-nosed fruit bats,
chunks.text: Most other nocturnal mammals respond to lunar intensity variations similarly to greater short-nosed fruit bats,
chunks.plain: Most night-active mammals behave the same way.

chunks.html: <mark class="turn">but</mark> mongoose lemurs (Eulemur mongoz) display the opposite pattern, as their heavy reliance on visual foraging results in a different balance of reward and risk.
chunks.text: but mongoose lemurs (Eulemur mongoz) display the opposite pattern, as their heavy reliance on visual foraging results in a different balance of reward and risk.
chunks.plain: Exception: lemurs do the opposite, because they find food by sight, so light pays off for them.

examples.say: A finding and its reason, then “most animals fit,” then one exception and its reason.

choices.t: It discusses two different responses to the same natural phenomenon, explains why one of those responses occurs, and then suggests that the other response still needs to be explained.
choices.why: Starts right, but the passage does explain the lemurs: “as their heavy reliance on visual foraging …”

choices.t: It describes and accounts for a finding, characterizes the finding as representative of a general pattern, and then describes and accounts for an exception to that pattern.
choices.why: Finding plus reason, then the general pattern, then the exception plus its reason: all three pieces match the tags.

choices.t: It presents and explains a study result, indicates that the result is similar to the results of many other studies, and then attributes a conflicting study result to a difference in that study’s methods.
choices.why: Starts right, but the lemur difference is put down to how lemurs forage, not to a study’s methods.

choices.t: It introduces an observation of a behavioral pattern, presents an explanation for the pattern, and then describes an exception to the pattern that casts doubt on that explanation.
choices.why: Starts right, but the exception is explained by the same weighing of reward and risk. It casts no doubt on it.

examples.lesson: Take away. For structure and purpose questions your tags are the answer. Then check every piece of the choice: three wrong choices here start correctly and fail on their last piece.

examples.title: Two texts
examples.question: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?
examples.jobans: The question asks how Text 2 would respond to a claim in Text 1 (the underlined claim is Text 1’s last sentence). Write one line for each text, then name the relationship.

chunks.head: Text 1
chunks.html: In 2007, a team led by Alice Storey analyzed a chicken bone found in El Arenal, Chile, dating it to 1321–1407 CE—over a century before Europeans invaded the region, bringing their own chickens.
chunks.text: In 2007, a team led by Alice Storey analyzed a chicken bone found in El Arenal, Chile, dating it to 1321–1407 CE—over a century before Europeans invaded the region, bringing their own chickens.
chunks.plain: A chicken bone from Chile dates from before Europeans arrived.

chunks.html: Storey also found that the El Arenal chicken shared a unique genetic mutation with the ancient chicken breeds of the Polynesian Islands in the Pacific.
chunks.text: Storey also found that the El Arenal chicken shared a unique genetic mutation with the ancient chicken breeds of the Polynesian Islands in the Pacific.
chunks.plain: It shares a mutation with old Polynesian chickens.

chunks.html: Thus, Polynesian peoples, not later Europeans, probably first introduced chickens to South America.

chunks.head: Text 2
chunks.html: An Australian research team weakened the case for a Polynesian origin for the El Arenal chicken by confirming that the mutation identified by Storey has occurred in breeds from around the world.
chunks.text: An Australian research team weakened the case for a Polynesian origin for the El Arenal chicken by confirming that the mutation identified by Storey has occurred in breeds from around the world.
chunks.plain: That mutation turns up worldwide, so it proves little.

chunks.html: More recently, <mark class="turn">though</mark>, a team led by Agusto Luzuriaga-Neira found that South American chicken breeds and Polynesian breeds share other genetic markers that European breeds lack.
chunks.text: More recently, though , a team led by Agusto Luzuriaga-Neira found that South American chicken breeds and Polynesian breeds share other genetic markers that European breeds lack.
chunks.plain: But newer work found other markers shared only by South American and Polynesian breeds.

chunks.text: Thus, the preponderance of evidence now favors a Polynesian origin.
chunks.plain: So the evidence now favors a Polynesian origin.

others.title: Words in Context
items: 221 ask for the word that fits a blank. 40 ask what a word means where it is used.
These are the shortest passages on the test: 53 words at the median. 79% of the fill-in choices are a single word.

What sets Easy apart is the sentence around the blank: 28 words at the median against 35 on Medium and 34 on Hard, with a contrast word in 21% against 37% and 32%. Medium and Hard look alike on both counts.

So: find the clue in the blank’s own sentence. If that sentence has a turn word, the clue is on the other side of it. Work out whether the blank should agree with the clue or go against it, put in your own plain word, then match.

others.title: Text Structure and Purpose
items: 54 ask for the main purpose, 29 for the overall structure, 66 for the function of an underlined part. 34% of the passages are stories, poems or plays.

Your tags are the answer. A structure answer is the tags in order (“then” marks a structure answer, but it does not pick the right one: in the bank it is in 25 of 29 right answers to overall-structure questions and 77 of 87 wrong ones). A function answer is the tag of the underlined sentence. A purpose answer says what the Point is there to do.
No function question is worked in this guide. In the bank, 100 questions point at an underlined part of the passage; read that part first, then ask what it does for the text around it.

others.title: Cross-Text Connections
items: Two short texts, 68 words each at the median. 42 questions ask how one author would respond to the other, 12 what both would agree on, 7 for a difference.
Of the 42 “respond” answers, 36 dispute, limit or qualify the other text (“not necessarily,” “overlooks,” “incomplete,” “yes, but”). Only 6 build on it.
So: write one line per text, then read Text 2 for the place where it pushes back. 56% of second texts contain a turn word.

others.title: Rhetorical Synthesis
items: A list of notes and a goal. Read the goal first: “The student wants to …” closes the notes in 203 of 204 questions.

When the goal is a difference or contrast (28 questions), the correct choice has a contrast word (but, whereas, while, unlike, than) in 96%, against 35% of wrong choices. When the goal is a similarity (17), it has both, like, also or similar in 82%, against 16%.

So: read the goal, then the four choices, and pick the one that does exactly what the goal asks. Wrong choices are often accurate and simply do something other than the goal, so accuracy alone does not decide. Reading only the goal and the choices, with the notes hidden, Claude picked College Board’s answer on 203 of the 204 questions; use the notes to check facts when two choices both seem to do the goal. Notes questions: goal first

othersIntro: The same four steps apply. What changes is where you look first.

intro: A routine only helps once it is automatic. Four drills, in this order, using the question IDs on the Practice sets page. This is a suggested plan, not a finding.
drills: Tag onlyTake ten passages and cover the choices. Tag every sentence and write its plain line. Aim for under 40 seconds a passage. Start with Easy inference and main idea questions.
Core firstTake ten Hard passages. For every sentence longer than three lines, write the core in about ten words, then list what each attachment adds.
Say before you lookDo ten questions with the choices covered. Write your Say line, uncover, choose. Count how often your line matched the answer.

The full routine, timedSets of nine questions in eleven minutes, which is test pace. For every miss, name the way the choice you picked was wrong, using the five kinds in Step 4, and keep a tally by job.

aparts.title: 1. A lead-in before the subject

pieces.text: To understand how temperature change affects microorganism-mediated cycling of soil nutrients in alpine ecosystems,
Eva Kaštovská et al. collected plant-soil cores
in the Tatra Mountains at elevations around 2,100 meters
and transplanted them
to elevations of 1,700–1,800 meters,
where the mean air temperature was warmer by 2°C.

aparts.core: Core in plain words. The team collected soil cores and moved them.
aparts.note: The sentence opens with “To understand …,” and the subject arrives only after the first comma. Jump to that comma, read the core, then come back. The lead-in tells you why they did it. The last add-on (“where … warmer by 2°C”) is the detail the whole passage turns on, so do not drop add-ons for good: read them second.

aparts.title: 2. An aside between dashes

pieces.text: Several scholars have argued that conditions in England in the late ninth through early eleventh centuries
—namely, burgeoning literacy amid running conflicts between England’s Anglo-Saxon kingdoms and Danish invaders—
were especially conducive to the production of the Old English epic poem Beowulf,
and they have dated the poem’s composition accordingly.

aparts.core: Core in plain words. Scholars argue that England in those centuries suited Beowulf, so they date it then.
aparts.note: Everything between the two dashes can be lifted out and the sentence still stands. “Namely” tells you the aside only spells out what “conditions” means. Then a second statement is joined on with “and.”

aparts.title: 3. A list of examples

pieces.text: However,
there is no evidence of significant spikes in carbon dioxide levels coinciding with relevant periods in sauropod evolution,
such as when the first large sauropods appeared, when several sauropod lineages underwent further evolution toward gigantism, or when sauropods reached their maximum known sizes,
suggesting that ______

aparts.core: Core in plain words. However, carbon dioxide did not spike at the key moments, suggesting that …
aparts.note: “Such as when …, when …, or when …” gives three examples of “relevant periods.” One is enough to get the idea. The core runs straight from “coinciding with relevant periods” to “suggesting that.”

aparts.title: 4. An “Although” lead-in

pieces.text: Although there is little genetic difference between river and cave A. mexicanus and all members of the species can emit the same sounds,
biologist Carole Hyacinthe and colleagues found that the context and significance of those sounds vary by location
—e.g., the click that river-dwelling A. mexicanus use to signal aggression is used by cave dwellers when foraging—
and the acoustic properties of cave fish sounds show some cave-specific variations as well.

aparts.core: Core in plain words. Hyacinthe’s team found that what the sounds mean varies by location, and cave sounds vary too.
aparts.note: A lead-in that starts with “Although” is the part the sentence is about to push past: it is true, but it is not the point. The point is the core that follows the comma.

aparts.title: 5. Brackets that define a word

pieces.text: To study how different agricultural land covers affect the species,
Rika Raffiudin and colleagues monitored the foraging activity of the bees as well as the pollen content of the honey from A. dorsata colonies at two sites in Indonesia:
Kampar, characterized by its surrounding monoculture farms
(growing a single crop),
and Kerinci, a forest-agriculture site where multiple crops,
including hot peppers and coffee,
are grown nearby.

aparts.core: Core in plain words. The team monitored bees and honey at two sites.
aparts.note: The bracket holds a definition; the commas around “including …” hold examples. “(growing a single crop)” is what “monoculture” means: if that word is new to you, read the bracket at once, because the whole question depends on it.

aparts.title: 6. Names, then a long aside, then the verb

pieces.text: Testing by Yuzo R. Yanagisuru, Otar Akanyeti, and James C. Liao using models of three head shapes
—narrow (low ratio of width to length), intermediate, and wide (high ratio of width to length)—
showed that
for medium-sized vortices,
fish with wide heads would be least able to distinguish between vortices and general turbulence in the water.

aparts.core: Core in plain words. Tests with model heads showed that wide-headed fish are worst at telling swirls from turbulence.
aparts.note: The verb (“showed”) comes long after the subject (“Testing …”): three names and a dash aside sit between them. Carry the subject across the dashes, and read the three names as “the team.”

aparts.title: 7. An older literary sentence
aparts.meta: 50 words · question e677fa6c · not a worked example

pieces.text: The land undulated very remarkably;
and my path,
for the last hour,
had wound about and about so confusedly,
in its effort to keep in the valleys,
that I no longer knew in what direction lay the sweet village of B——,
where I had determined to stop for the night.

aparts.core: Core in plain words. The land rolled up and down, and my path twisted so much that I no longer knew which way the village was.
aparts.note: Two statements joined by a semicolon. In the second, the subject (“my path”) is cut off from its verb (“had wound”) by “for the last hour,” and the result arrives after “so confusedly … that.”

checkBlocks.p: Read each choice against the passage, not against the other choices.

list: Split the choice at its joints: although, but, and, because, which. Each piece needs a line in the passage, or a cell in the table, that you can point to.
The whole choice has to do the job. A true statement that does not answer this question is wrong.
One false piece and the choice is out. You do not have to find everything that is wrong with it.

methodExtra: Two bases. The 5 plain look-up table questions have no claim or blank, so the turn-word, cue and choice-wording figures are out of the other 550. The letter shares are out of all 555.
turnNote: Table or graph counts the 128 questions with a blank or a claim; the 5 plain look-ups are left out.
method: Source. An export of College Board’s SAT Suite Question Bank: 1,845 Reading and Writing questions with College Board’s explanations. The reading part of this guide covers the 1,230 that are not grammar or transitions (those are in the Grammar section).

Measured by script on all 555 Information and Ideas questions. Passage and sentence lengths, turn words, where the blank sits, the cue before the blank, choice lengths and letters. These figures were computed from the bank by script.

Read one by one. 98 questions (294 wrong choices) for how wrong choices fail. All 83 support and weaken passages for where the claim sits, checked twice. All 40 literary-quotation claims. The 42 “respond” answers in cross-text questions, with the 14 unclear ones read in full.
A second opinion. 15 of those questions were also labeled in a separate pass that did not see the first labels. It chose the same kind of flaw for 42 of 45 wrong choices.

The routine itself is a recommendation. The counts say where the claim, the blank and the long sentences are. They do not prove that these four steps raise a score. Practice is what will show that for you.
The one-by-one sample leans Hard (52% of it, against 43% of the bank), so its shares describe harder questions best.
The tags and the five kinds of wrong choice are categories made for this guide. College Board does not use them.
Counts made by pattern matching (attachments in long sentences, two-part choices, cautious and strong words) are approximate.
The export keeps neither underlining nor graph images, so no function question and no graph question is worked here. Graph questions are still counted and listed.
Everything describes this bank. A future test can differ.
